title: Coproduction and evaluation of a self-management intervention for post-stroke fatigue
official: COproduction and evaluation of a self-MAnagemenT intervention for post-stroke Fatigue: Feasibility study (work package 4)
summary:
Experiencing fatigue (lack of energy, tiredness) is very common after stroke and mini-stroke (TIA). Fatigue makes it difficult for people to take part in everyday activities. Many people describe fatigue as the most difficult and upsetting problem caused by their stroke. We don’t know the best way to manage fatigue after stroke and many people don’t receive any information or support. We have developed an online self-management programme to help people better manage their fatigue after stroke. In this study we will test whether the fatigue programme is practical and acceptable. We will also look at whether the study design is convenient before completing a larger trial to test whether the programme helps to improve fatigue for stroke patients.

Patients may be able to take part in the study if they:
1. Are aged 18 years or over
2. Had a stroke or mini-stroke within the past 6 - 24 months
3. Are experiencing fatigue since their stroke or mini-stroke
4. Live in an area where the study is running

Everyone who takes part in the study will receive access to the online fatigue programme. Study participants will be asked to complete a questionnaire at the start of the study. They will then be asked to complete the online fatigue programme over 6 weeks and attend a 30-minute appointment with a healthcare provider after this. The appointment may be in person or via phone or video call. After 3 months, participants will be asked to complete a final questionnaire.

Background and study aims
Many people experience ongoing tiredness after a stroke or transient ischaemic attack (TIA, sometimes called a mini-stroke). Fatigue can affect everyday activities, mood, work, relationships, and quality of life. Despite this, many people receive little information or support to help manage their fatigue.
Researchers, stroke survivors, and healthcare professionals have worked together to develop a new self-management programme called Rethink Fatigue. The programme is delivered through a digital app and aims to help people understand and manage post-stroke fatigue.
The aim of this study is to find out whether the programme is acceptable to people with stroke-related fatigue, whether the study procedures work well, and whether it will be suitable to do a larger trial in the future.
 
Who can participate? 
People may be able to take part if they:
1. Are aged 18 years or over
2. Had a stroke or TIA between 6 and 24 months ago
3. Experience fatigue that affects their daily life
4. Can understand English
5. Live within the study catchment area
6. Can give informed consent
 
What does the study involve? 
Participants will:
1. Complete consent and baseline questionnaires
2. Receive access to the Rethink Fatigue digital programme, which contains six sessions designed to be completed over 6 weeks
3. Receive reminders and support if needed
4. Attend a follow-up appointment with a trained healthcare professional around 8–10 weeks after starting the programme
5. Complete questionnaires about their experiences and fatigue at approximately 3 months
6. Some participants may be invited to take part in an interview to discuss their experience of the programme and study
 
What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Participants may benefit from learning new strategies to help understand and manage their fatigue. They may also value contributing to research that could improve support for future stroke survivors.
The study is considered low risk. The intervention consists of a digital self-management programme and a healthcare professional follow-up appointment. No significant risks are expected, although participants may find some questions or discussions about their health and fatigue upsetting or tiring. Participants can choose not to answer any question and can withdraw from the study at any time.
 
Where is the study run from? 
The study is coordinated by the Birmingham Clinical Trials Unit (BCTU), University of Birmingham (UK). Participants will be recruited through primary care, community services and hospital services across the West Midlands.
 
When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
August 2026 to February 2027
 
Who is funding the study? 
The study is funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) and the Stroke Association through the NIHR Programme Grants for Applied Research programme (Grant Reference: NIHR205012)
 
Who is the main contact? 
1. Dr Grace Turner, G.Turner.1@bham.ac.uk
2. COMbAT Fatigue Study Team, COMbATFatigueStudy@trials.bham.ac.uk

interventions.name:
The intervention consists of:
1. Rethink Fatigue – a digital self-management programme for post-stroke fatigue comprising of six core sessions delivered over 6 weeks, plus a caregiver session and additional resources 
2. A healthcare professional follow-up appointment delivered between weeks 8 and 1

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1. Diagnosis of stroke or TIA occurring within 6-24 months prior to enrollment (first or recurrent)
2. Fatigue impacting on daily life, defined by answering “yes” to both of the Greater Manchester Stroke Assessment Tool fatigue questions: “Do you feel tired all the time or get tired very quickly since your stroke or mini-stroke (TIA)?” and “Would you like additional help and support for this?”
3. Adults aged >=18 years
4. Ability to understand English
5. Resident in catchment area for the sites
6. Ability to provide fully informed consent for participation in the study (with or without support)
Exclusion criteria:
1. Taking part in a fatigue course within the past 12 months†
2. Diagnosis of dementia (identified from medical records*)
3. Receiving palliative care (identified from medical records*)

† Note: For the purposes of exclusion, a formal course or programme delivered either online or in person would qualify as a ‘fatigue course’. This would not include ad hoc advice, or provision of information, e.g., a leaflet

* Note: For participants who self-refer to the study, we will not have access to medical records; therefore, taking a pragmatic approach, these criteria will be self-confirmed by the participant
